claims.text: The starting material is commercial Ti-6Al-4V with a conventional microstructure.
Optimized plasma nitriding will produce a uniform, nanocrystalline TiN-enriched surface layer on Ti-6Al-4V.
Plasma nitriding will increase the surface hardness of Ti-6Al-4V by more than 50% relative to the untreated alloy.
Plasma nitriding will significantly reduce the wear rate of Ti-6Al-4V relative to the untreated alloy.
The hardness and wear improvements will hold during sliding at room temperature through 150 °C.
Optimized plasma nitriding can provide the proposed surface improvements without compromising the alloy's bulk properties.
The proposed treatment uses a low-pressure N2/H2 atmosphere at approximately 600 °C for 10–12 hours, with subsequent parameter optimization.
Optimization of temperature, duration, and gas composition will enable controllable nitrogen diffusion and uniform TiN formation.
The modified surface will contain finely dispersed TiN precipitates in a diffusion-hardened matrix.
Plasma nitriding will induce compressive residual stresses in the surface layer.
During plasma nitriding, nitrogen ions diffuse into the near-surface of Ti-6Al-4V and form TiN precipitates.
Precipitated reinforcing phases such as the proposed TiN can strengthen the alloy surface.
TiN precipitates and compressive residual stresses obstruct dislocation movement.
Obstruction of dislocation movement and surface reinforcement mitigate abrasive wear and increase wear resistance.
The enhanced properties are confined to the nitrided surface layer.
Poorly optimized nitriding can cause near-surface or bulk microstructural changes that compromise toughness or fatigue resistance.
Ball-on-disc testing at temperatures up to 150 °C can characterize sliding wear and abrasive wear behavior.
